extracted.intended_audience: litigators, judges, and legal professionals handling unfair-competition/copyright disputes between news services
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a courtroom hearing (Associated Press v. International News Service) discussing legal standards and factual criteria for claims that one news service misappropriated another's news (taking from bulletin boards/early editions/rewrite). Focus is on equitable relief, proof, industry custom, and corporate liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intangible property in news / exchangeability
rubrics_metrics.description: The great value of the complainant's business lies in the exchangeability of his tanks. This quality the complainant has created itself, and no one has the right to appropriate it as his own. That quality is incorporeal and intangible, but it is property nevertheless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames news/service value as intangible property whose 'exchangeability' is commercially valuable. Use when assessing whether news content or the business model merits protection as proprietary, even absent a conventional copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to equitable relief when no adequate remedy at law
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff manifestly having no adequate remedy at law, is entitled to have his property protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports seeking an injunction where legal remedies (damages) are inadequate because harm is to an incorporeal business interest; courts will consider whether equitable relief is appropriate based on adequacy of legal remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of injunction: taking news from published newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole kernel of this case is in the third prayer for relief, in which it is sought to prevent us from taking news from the newspapers as published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key legal question is whether courts may enjoin copying/taking of news after publication (e.g., from early editions or bulletin boards). Evaluate whether requested injunction would forbid commonly accepted newsgathering practices and whether law supports such a novel restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry custom as defense (copying from early editions/bulletin boards)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is done on all news associations by all newspapers, and it is a uniform custom without any exception whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longstanding, widespread industry practices (scanning early editions, copying from bulletin boards/early papers) may be offered as a defense or to show that a requested new rule of law is inconsistent with established custom. Consider historic practice and reciprocity among services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of moral condemnation as substitute for legal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to inject into this case a moral issue, and charge us with moral delinquency, is a mere pretext... it is sought... to graft upon the law, an entirely new principle, and one contrary to that established by all the other authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguing moral wrongfulness alone is insufficient; courts require legal doctrine and authority. Be cautious about appeals to morality when seeking to expand legal protection beyond precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published foreign dispatches / simultaneous publication not giving exclusive statutory right
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that this was not such a copyright of the special matter obtained under the contract, and such a simultaneous publication as to give the Tribune an exclusive right under the statute, to publish the same in the United States, and that it was not entitled to an injunction to restrain The Associated Press from taking such matter from the columns of the Times, after its publication in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where material is published abroad (or otherwise publicly available) and published simultaneously or nearly simultaneously, statutory copyright/exclusive injunctions may not lie. Use precedent to evaluate claims based on foreign/earlier publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate liability requires knowledge/consent or arrangements with employees/agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the defendant nor any of its officers and employees has, to my knowledge, or with my consent, arranged with any telegraph operator, or any other employee ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To impute employee misconduct to a corporation or to show systemic wrongdoing, plaintiff should show knowledge, consent, or specific arrangements by officers/management. Denials of corporate knowledge are a defense; courts examine whether officer-level knowledge/consent can be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence / delay in complaining undermines claim
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1915 ... until we were served with the papers in this case. The Associated Press ... made no complaint to the American. They made no complaint to us. There has never been a complaint made by them throughout the history of our relations of any of the things which they embody in this complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long history of mutual practice without complaint may undercut equity claims (stigma, sudden enforcement); consider laches, acquiescence, and the timing of the suit when assessing relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits and evidence quality: need for source identification and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: The imputation against us is made on affidavits of affiants who do not even give the source of their information, and cannot tell the names of the people who are supposed to have done this thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits alleging theft/misconduct should specify sources, names, and facts; bare suspicion or anonymous assertions weaken proof. Courts scrutinize affidavits for corroboration and direct evidence rather than vague allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of systematic practice (employment of agents to capture early-edition items / premiums)
rubrics_metrics.description: You will see from these affidavits that they employed men for the special purpose of doing this particular work, of getting all this information from whatever source, from our news, and everybody else's news ... the affidavits on the part of the complainants show that they pay a premium to people who get those stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that a party systematically employed people to obtain prepublication material or paid premiums for such tips supports a finding of deliberate misappropriation. Evaluate payrolls, instructions, communications, and payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market power and membership/by-law practices relevant to unfair competition/antitrust concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: They are so intrenched and so organized, that it would be practically impossible for anybody to start a newspaper. You could not start a morning paper ... because it requires the unanimous consent of the members in the locality before another member can get in ... the Attorney General ... recommended that certain unlawful features of those by-laws were eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate structure, by-laws, membership rules, and exclusionary practices can bear on claims of monopoly or unfair competition. Examine whether by-laws arbitrarily fix charges or bar entry, and consider prior governmental/AG findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable balancing: practical consequences of injunction on business and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If this injunction was granted to the fullest extent that they ask for, that they would cut you off very much, excepting as they allege, illegal practices, and copying from bulletin boards, and the early editions of other papers ... It would be a sad thing in this country, Your Honor, if we had to rely upon one news service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh the practical effects of equitable relief (e.g., shutting down a competitor, reducing public access to news). Assess whether injunctive relief would unduly harm the defendant's business or detract from public interest in diverse news sources.
